title: Same area and different boundaries
sections: Use n≥1 unit squares, without overlap, connected by full shared sides. Count all exposed unit edges, including hole edges. If e is the number of shared sides, then P=4n−2e: each meeting removes two edge contributions. Hence every perimeter is even. Adding a tile touching k old sides changes P by 4−2k.

Maximum: Connectivity gives e≥n−1, so P≤2n+2; a straight row attains it. Equality holds exactly when the tile-adjacency graph is a tree. This rules out a 2-by-2 block, but does not rule out every hole: corner contacts can seal a hole without adding a shared side.

Minimum: If r rows and c columns are occupied, then P≥2(r+c) and n≤rc. For P=2s, the largest possible area is floor(s/2)·ceil(s/2), attained by a balanced rectangle. For fixed n, the minimum perimeter is 2 ceil(2√n). Near-square rectangles with corner-started partial strips attain the bound for every n. Equality in P≥2(r+c) requires one occupied interval in every occupied row and column, not necessarily a full rectangle.
K–1: Build legal shapes, count exposed sides and compare records. The shared launch models both a whole-side join and boundary counting with three tiles.
Grades 2–3: Track shared-side cancellation and one-tile changes, then explain a longest-boundary construction.
Grades 4–5: Pair row/column lower bounds with attaining shapes and generalize exact area–perimeter limits. Square-root notation is an optional adult shorthand.

A best shape found so far is a record and a candidate optimum. A conjecture predicts it cannot be beaten. A matching lower or upper bound, together with a construction attaining it, proves the optimum. The detailed counting arguments remain on printed page 3.
